passage: At the team dinner in a Lower Parel restaurant, Urmila watched Kashish's boyfriend, Ankur, arrive late and, within minutes, mock her order in front of everyone. "Can I say one thing, and then I'll drop it?"

Tonight I just said, "The phenyl days seem rough for you. I'll keep the window open." He looked at me for a second and nodded. He didn't explain. I didn't ask.

I'm writing because I can't make sense of today and you're the only one who won't rush me.

It wasn't about Shalini's father. It was Ma. I was eight when she died. I was the one who stood there with the flowers. I thought that was long done, packed away. I haven't cried about her in fifteen years.

It's late, and I'm writing instead of pretending I'm fine, which is new for me.

Today at the mall they had a big banner for Father's Day, and a little girl was choosing a card with her dad. I stood there and started crying. Over a card. It's been twelve years since Baba left us, and I thought I'd sealed that away.

Bidisha

Counsellor's note, Class 10, Tuesday.
Aadhya came to see me today, upset. She got new glasses last week and is convinced the whole class mocks her. "They all stare. Wasim was laughing at me in maths." I asked what exactly Wasim had done. She said he turned around and smiled. I checked, gently, with the maths teacher: Wasim had been laughing at a joke on the board. When I asked Aadhya what she herself thinks of the glasses, she said, quietly, "They make me look like an owl." I think much of the staring she feels is her own worry about her looks, felt as others' contempt. What I did next: I didn't tell her she was wrong. I asked her to write down, for one week, every time someone actually says something about the glasses. We'll look at the list together next Tuesday.
